title: Quantum Computing
summary: Computing with amplitudes. Entanglement is the threshold: multi-qubit states that cannot be described one qubit at a time. Speed-ups come from interference steering amplitude toward right answers, not from trying every answer at once.
sources: Nielsen & Chuang: Quantum Computation and Quantum Information
Preskill: Quantum Computing in the NISQ era and beyond (2018)
Grover: A fast quantum mechanical algorithm for database search (1996)

nodes.label: Qubits & Superposition
nodes.summary: A qubit's state is α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with |α|² + |β|² = 1; amplitudes, not probabilities, are what evolve.
nodes.outcome: Write a normalised qubit state and compute measurement probabilities.
nodes.check: A qubit is √0.8|0⟩ + √0.2|1⟩. What is the probability of measuring 0?

nodes.label: Measurement & the Born Rule
nodes.summary: Measuring gives one outcome with probability |amplitude|² and collapses the state; repeated runs (shots) estimate probabilities.
nodes.outcome: Estimate a probability from shot counts and its uncertainty.
nodes.check: After measuring a qubit and getting 1, what do you get if you measure it again immediately?
nodes.answer: 1 again: measurement collapsed the state to |1⟩.

nodes.label: The Bloch Sphere
nodes.summary: Single-qubit pure states as points on a sphere; gates are rotations.
nodes.outcome: Place |0⟩, |1⟩, |+⟩ and |−⟩ on the Bloch sphere.
nodes.check: Where on the Bloch sphere is the state |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2?
nodes.answer: On the equator, on the +x axis.

nodes.label: Single-Qubit Gates
nodes.summary: X (bit flip), Z (phase flip), H (Hadamard) and rotations: unitary, reversible operations.
nodes.outcome: Predict the output of a short gate sequence on |0⟩.
nodes.check: What do you get applying H twice to |0⟩?
nodes.answer: |0⟩ again: H is its own inverse.

nodes.label: Interference
nodes.summary: Amplitudes can be negative, so paths can cancel. H·H = I is interference: the |1⟩ paths cancel. Every quantum speed-up is engineered interference.
nodes.outcome: Explain H·H|0⟩ = |0⟩ as two paths to |1⟩ cancelling.
nodes.check: Why can two quantum paths to the same outcome make that outcome less likely, unlike classical probabilities?
nodes.answer: Amplitudes can be negative, so they can cancel (destructive interference); probabilities can only add.

nodes.label: "Quantum computers try every answer at once"
nodes.summary: Measurement returns one outcome; without interference that boosts right answers, a superposition is no better than random guessing.
nodes.outcome: Explain why superposition alone gives no speed-up.
nodes.check: You put n qubits in superposition over all inputs and measure. What do you get?
nodes.answer: One random input; the speed-up needs interference to amplify the right answer before measuring.

nodes.label: Entanglement
nodes.summary: Joint states like (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 that cannot be written as a product of single-qubit states; outcomes are correlated however far apart.
nodes.outcome: Show the Bell state is not a product state and predict joint measurements.
nodes.check: In the Bell state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, the first qubit is measured as 1. What will the second qubit give?

nodes.label: "Entanglement sends messages faster than light"
nodes.summary: Each side alone sees random outcomes; the correlation is only visible when results are compared over a classical channel (no-signalling).
nodes.outcome: Explain the no-signalling theorem with a Bell pair.
nodes.check: Can Alice send Bob a message instantly by measuring her half of an entangled pair?
nodes.answer: No: Bob's results look random on their own; correlations appear only after classical communication.

nodes.label: Multi-Qubit Gates & Circuits
nodes.summary: CNOT and controlled gates; H then CNOT makes a Bell pair. Circuits are read left to right.
nodes.outcome: Build a Bell-state circuit and trace its state.
nodes.check: Which two gates, applied to |00⟩, create a Bell state?
nodes.answer: A Hadamard on the first qubit, then a CNOT with the first qubit as control.

nodes.label: No-Cloning & Quantum Cryptography
nodes.summary: Unknown quantum states cannot be copied, which makes eavesdropping detectable (BB84).
nodes.outcome: Explain how BB84 detects an eavesdropper.
nodes.check: Why does an eavesdropper on a BB84 key exchange get caught?
nodes.answer: Measuring the qubits disturbs them (no-cloning), so errors appear when Alice and Bob compare a sample of bits.

nodes.label: Quantum Algorithms
nodes.summary: Deutsch–Jozsa, Grover (√N search), Shor (factoring): each wins by interference, not brute parallelism.
nodes.outcome: State the speed-up of Grover's algorithm and why it is quadratic.
nodes.check: Grover's algorithm searches N unsorted items in about how many steps?

nodes.label: Decoherence & Noise
nodes.summary: Interaction with the environment destroys superposition; T1 and T2 times bound how long a computation can run.
nodes.outcome: Estimate how many gates fit inside a coherence time.
nodes.check: A qubit's coherence time is 100 µs and each gate takes 50 ns. Roughly how many gates fit?

nodes.label: Quantum Error Correction
nodes.summary: Encode one logical qubit in many physical qubits and measure syndromes without measuring the data (surface codes).
nodes.outcome: Explain how syndrome measurement finds an error without collapsing the data.
nodes.check: Why can't quantum error correction just copy a qubit three times like a classical repetition code?
nodes.answer: No-cloning forbids copying an unknown state; instead information is spread across entangled qubits and errors found via syndromes.

nodes.label: Quantum Hardware
nodes.summary: Superconducting circuits, trapped ions, photons and neutral atoms trade speed, fidelity, connectivity and scale.
nodes.outcome: Compare two hardware platforms on gate speed, fidelity and connectivity.
nodes.check: Why are superconducting qubits kept near absolute zero?
nodes.answer: To make the circuit superconducting and suppress thermal noise that would destroy the quantum state.
